nameStory: The "striped" in striped goosefoot refers to the distinctive light-colored stripes or veins that run along the green leaves, creating a zebra-like pattern. Like other goosefoots, the name comes from the supposed resemblance of the leaf shape to a goose's webbed foot, though you might need to squint a bit to see it!
description: Striped goosefoot is an annual herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with branching stems and distinctive striped leaves. This member of the amaranth family produces small, inconspicuous greenish flowers in dense clusters. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance but stands out due to its uniquely patterned foliage. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Diamond to lance-shaped leaves with prominent light green or whitish stripes running parallel to the leaf veins, creating a distinctive striped pattern against the darker green background

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers without petals, clustered in dense, branched spikes at stem tips and leaf joints - they feel rough and granular to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant reaching 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat succulent and may have a reddish tinge

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, lens-shaped black seeds that are shiny and smooth when rubbed between your fingers, enclosed in papery coverings

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves feel slightly thick and waxy with a powdery coating that can rub off on your fingers, and they're arranged alternately on the stem

habitat: Striped goosefoot favors disturbed soils in sunny locations, particularly around gardens, roadsides, and waste areas. It prefers rich, well-drained soils and is often found near agricultural areas or residential developments. Given its extreme rarity in New England, any habitat where it appears should be considered exceptional.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring with the characteristic striped leaves already visible, though they start quite small and compact.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the plant reaches full height and the striped leaf pattern is most pronounced. Flowers appear in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and the plant begins to turn yellow and brown, though the striped pattern may still be visible on younger leaves.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant dies completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to potentially germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite being in the amaranth family, striped goosefoot is actually closely related to beets, spinach, and quinoa - you could theoretically eat the young leaves, though given how rare this plant is in New England, you'd want to admire it rather than harvest it!
confusionNotes: The distinctive leaf striping makes this species quite unique among New England plants, but it could potentially be confused with other goosefoots when young. Look for those telltale light stripes - no other goosefoot in our region has this zebra-like leaf pattern.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is extraordinarily rare in New England with only one documented observation, making it more of a botanical curiosity than a common find. The scientific name 'betaceum' hints at its relationship to beets (Beta species), reflecting the close family connections within what used to be called the goosefoot family before it was merged into the larger amaranth family.
compareHints: Unlike the common lambsquarters with its plain green leaves dusted with white powder, striped goosefoot has those unmistakable light stripes running through each leaf. It's also typically smaller than tree spinach and lacks the thick, succulent stems of some desert goosefoots. The striping is really the dead giveaway that sets it apart from all its goosefoot cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common lambsquarters is much more widespread than its relatives like pitseed goosefoot or fig-leaved goosefoot in New England.
Among New England goosefoots, pitseed goosefoot stands out for its strongly toothed lower leaves and honeycomb-pitted seeds.
Fogg's goosefoot is distinguished from Common Lambsquarters by having more triangular, less elongated leaves and typically being smaller overall.
Unlike common lambsquarters which has simple diamond or triangular leaves, fig-leaved goosefoot has deeply divided, lobed leaves that are unmistakable.

Desert goosefoot stands out from other New England goosefoots primarily by its exceptionally powdery texture - much more pronounced than the light dustiness of common lambsquarters or other relatives.
Tree spinach dwarfs its goosefoot relatives like common lambsquarters, which rarely exceed 3-4 feet tall and have much thinner stems.
